title: Keeping two boxes at once
idea: You can have several variables, each with its own name and value. Each box keeps its own value.

exercises.prompt:
What does this show?

apples = 3
bananas = 5
print(apples)
print(bananas)
exercises.explanation: Two boxes, two values. print(apples) shows 3; print(bananas) shows 5. Each box keeps its own value.

exercises.prompt: A program can have more than one variable at the same time.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Each variable is its own box with its own name and value.

exercises.prompt:
Two boxes:

cats = 2
dogs = 4

What does print(dogs) show?
exercises.explanation: print(dogs) opens the dogs box, which holds 4. The cats box is separate.

exercises.prompt:
Each box holds its own value. Match the variable to what print shows.

red = 1
blue = 8
exercises.explanation: Each name opens its own box: red holds 1, blue holds 8.

exercises.prompt:
What does this show?

first = 10
second = 20
print(second)
print(first)
exercises.explanation: Order of the print lines decides what shows first: second (20), then first (10).

exercises.prompt: You already stored width and height. Build a line that shows the value of height.
exercises.explanation: print(height) opens the height box and shows its value. The width box is untouched.

exercises.prompt: Storing a value in one variable also changes the value in another variable.
exercises.explanation: No. Each box is separate. Filling one box does not touch any other box.

exercises.prompt: Put these lines in order: store two values, then show both (pens first, then erasers).
exercises.explanation: Fill both boxes first, then read them. Reading order sets the output order.

exercises.prompt: Review from earlier units: print("Hello") shows what?
exercises.explanation: Quotes mean plain text, shown exactly: Hello. (No box involved here.)

exercises.prompt: Spot the mix-up. Which print shows the VALUE 5, given 'coins = 5'?
exercises.explanation: Only print(coins) — no quotes — opens the box and shows its value, 5.
